title: CHAPTER 16: TRIBAL, PEASANT & CIVIL REBELLIONS UNDER BRITISH RULE

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Civil rebellions were primarily led by ousted rulers, displaced landlords, and religious leaders against British territorial expansion and high revenue demands.
Peasant movements focused specifically against oppressive zamindars, exorbitant land rents, moneylenders, and forced commercial cultivation such as indigo.
Tribal uprisings were triggered by the intrusion of outsiders (dikus), loss of traditional forest rights, and the introduction of British judicial systems.
The Santhal Rebellion (1855–56), led by Sidhu and Kanhu, resulted in the creation of the separate Santhal Parganas district.
Birsa Munda led the 'Ulgulan' (Great Tumult) in the Chota Nagpur region, aiming to establish Munda rule and regain traditional land rights.

blocks.content: British colonial rule in India was marked by continuous resistance from different sections of society. Apart from major revolts like 1857, numerous tribal, peasant, and civil rebellions erupted throughout the 18th and 19th centuries. These movements were expressions of deep economic exploitation, administrative oppression, land revenue policies, and cultural interference by the British. Although most of these rebellions were localised and unorganised, they played a crucial role in shaping Indian nationalism. For SSC examinations, this chapter is important because questions are frequently asked on causes, leaders, regions, and nature of these movements.
Tribal revolts were mainly reactions against British forest policies, land alienation, moneylenders, missionaries, and the destruction of traditional tribal life.

The Santhal rebellion was one of the most powerful tribal uprisings against British rule. It occurred in the Rajmahal Hills region (present-day Jharkhand and Bihar). The Santhals rose against zamindars, moneylenders, and British officials.
Leaders: Sidhu and Kanhu
Causes: Exploitation by moneylenders, land alienation, high rents Outcome: Brutally suppressed but led to the creation of Santhal Pargana
Led by Birsa Munda, the Munda revolt aimed at establishing Munda Raj and ending British control. Birsa mobilised tribals against forced labour (begar) and land alienation.
Outcome: Suppressed after Birsa’s arrest; led to Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908)
The tribal uprisings were primarily directed against the dikus or outsiders who exploited the indigenous population under British protection.
The Kol rebellion took place in Chotanagpur region against British administration and outsiders. It was caused by the transfer of tribal land to non-tribals.
Peasant movements arose due to oppressive land revenue systems, high rents, eviction of peasants, and exploitation by zamindars and indigo planters.
The Indigo Revolt occurred in Bengal when peasants refused to grow indigo for European planters. Planters forced peasants to cultivate indigo under exploitative conditions.
Outcome: Indigo Commission (1860) acknowledged planter exploitation

rows: Outsiders (Dikus), British Forest Officials, Revenue Agents
High revenue rates, eviction from land, forced crop cultivation
Encroachment on forest rights, land alienation, forced labor (begar)
Local agrarian leaders, religious reformers, ruined landlords
Messianic charismatic tribal leaders (e.g., Birsa Munda, Sidhu-Kanhu)

blocks.content: The Deccan riots took place in Maharashtra against moneylenders. Peasants attacked moneylenders’ houses and destroyed debt records.
Outcome: Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act (1879)
The Moplah rebellion occurred in Malabar region of Kerala. It was caused by agrarian grievances combined with religious factors.
Civil rebellions were led by deposed rulers, zamindars, and local chiefs who lost power and privileges under British rule.
This rebellion occurred in Bengal during the late 18th century. Sanyasis and Fakirs rose against British restrictions on movement and heavy taxation.

items: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's famous novel 'Anandamath' is set against the backdrop of the Sanyasi Rebellion (1763–1800).
Dinabandhu Mitra authored the famous Bengali play 'Neel Darpan' (1860) to depict the severe exploitation of Indigo farmers.
The Santhal Parganas Tenancy Act was passed following the Santhal Hul of 1855 to safeguard tribal lands from non-tribal alienation.

blocks.content: The Poligars of Tamil Nadu rebelled against British revenue policies and annexation.
Though these revolts failed militarily, they exposed the exploitative nature of British rule. They strengthened anti-colonial consciousness and laid the foundation for organised national movements.
Lack of unity, absence of modern weapons, limited leadership, and strong British military power led to the failure of these movements.
